1. Strange lights

Strange lights are appearing over the town

The False Rapture Editorial pick

People under the lights become weightless and start giving away their possessions, convinced an ascension is imminent. Footage shows the beams collecting laughter rather than souls: a stranded angel has mistaken the town’s sarcastic complaints for sincere requests to leave Earth. Its rescue vessel cannot carry bodies, only personalities. The investigators demonstrate the difference between wanting to die and wanting a day off by bringing the angel to a miserable staff meeting. It returns everyone intact and grants the town one actual paid holiday, terrifying local employers.

The angel's misreading of workplace despair ties supernatural danger directly to the game's sardonic premise, and the staff meeting earns a memorable practical payoff.

2. The Sky Is Leaking

The lights fall into gardens as tiny suns, making tomatoes ripen instantly and tools melt. A broken weather balloon turns out to have punctured the translucent body of an enormous sleeping animal curled around the atmosphere; each light is a clot, and the balloon recovery firm has been harvesting them. The investigators return the stolen clots using the firm’s own launch equipment before the animal wakes and shakes Earth loose. The firm loses its miraculous energy contract, and the town spends winter eating suspiciously warm tomatoes.

The falling suns yield strong physical clues and an unusual ecological explanation; returning stolen clots reverses the established cause rather than inventing a last-minute rescue.

Notes
C01-P03

3. The Opening Act

The lights answer marching-band practice, but recordings reveal they keep correcting one particularly bad trumpet part. Ancient accounts identify the visitors as touring aliens who mistake rehearsals for an invitation to perform; their opening note would rupture every human lung. With promised agency linguists never answering, the investigators translate the warning through musical imitation and stage a deliberately terrible audition. The disappointed aliens cancel Earth’s gig, leaving a scathing review and one instrument that can safely play their lethal frequency.

The deliberate bad audition turns the document's musical contact idea into an actionable comic solution, with particularly good amateur-investigator fit.

Notes
C01-P01

4. Night Shift Pollinators

The lights appear over streetlamps, then households wake to glowing eggs in their ceilings. A blacked-out warehouse contains enormous transparent moths that use artificial light to mistake buildings for flowers; the eggs will hatch into larvae that eat the electromagnetic field keeping local matter solid. The team discovers the moths navigate by the true moon and persuades the town to switch off everything for one night. The swarm leaves peacefully, while investigators spend the blackout manually answering complaints that HQ’s nonexistent pest department should have handled.

Artificial-light behavior supports a clear discovery chain and collective blackout solution, though the larval threat is more abstract than the strongest reveals.

C01-P06

5. Lanterns for the Missing

Every light stops over a house whose occupant has disappeared, while residents insist those people never existed. Following a discarded birthday card exposes a celestial scavenger that consumes people and their place in memory, leaving its glowing digestive organs overhead. The investigators preserve names by reading them over the town’s emergency speakers, forcing the creature to regurgitate its victims. It flees hungry; everyone remembers the missing neighbors, including their debts, and the team’s sole reimbursement is an unsolicited casserole.

The names broadcast gives an emotionally satisfying rescue with a mundane reimbursement joke, but memory-erasing predators recur across the collection.

Notes
C01-P02

6. The Search Party

The lights inspect dumpsters and swimming pools, ignoring military targets while abducting anything shaped like a jellyfish. The investigators trace their search to an alien teenager who escaped a family vacation and is hiding as a local convenience-store clerk. His parents plan to sterilize the town to shake him out. The team gets him to reveal himself by confronting the real reason he fled: he was promised a summer internship on a slave planet. They negotiate his first ordinary wage instead, and the embarrassed parents depart with several regrettable human souvenirs.

The ridiculous search targets and exploited alien teenager provide humane comedy; the parents' willingness to cancel sterilization could use a sharper causal hinge.

C01-P09

7. Future Fireworks

The lights precisely trace tomorrow’s accidents, although residents interpret the displays as a tourist attraction. An investigator recognizes their own impending death in the pattern, then finds a retired emergency dispatcher communicating backward through an electrical storm. She is the lone survivor of a catastrophe caused by the town’s new power plant and has only one night left to change it. The team evacuates the plant and cuts its cooling test short; the lights become an ordinary sunset, erasing both disaster and the dispatcher’s warning career.

Recognizable emergency details make the warning investigable and the intervention complete, although backward disaster prevention is a familiar engine.

Notes
C01-P04

8. Second-Hand Stars

Each light appears after somebody buys a cheap lamp at a clearance sale, and illuminated rooms become windows onto different historical nights. The lamps contain captive stars sold by a sorcerer who financed immortality by stripping constellations; opening all of them will collapse the town’s timeline into his private midnight. Rather than wait for a nonexistent temporal unit, the team returns the lamps to the sky during the sale’s grand finale. The sorcerer ages centuries in seconds, and the rescued stars spell a thank-you visible only from the parking lot.

Second-hand lamps and captive stars give appealing everyday contrast, but the timeline collapse and return procedure need more connective explanation.

9. The Town in the Fishbowl

The lights stay fixed despite wind, and telescope images show enormous fingers behind them. A child’s missing goldfish has grown into a cosmic pet and is observing the town inside a bowl stolen from a vanished agency depot; the apparent stars are its aquarium toys. Each feeding brings a tide through downtown. The investigators reconstruct the owner’s familiar feeding whistle, coax the fish away, and smash the bowl’s miniature Earth replica to release the real town. The child wants compensation for her fish, which now occupies the moon’s far side.

A cosmic goldfish is memorably absurd, though the bowl replica's relationship to the actual town makes the decisive escape less intuitive.

10. Light at the End of the World

The lights extinguish whenever someone dies, and the newest ones resemble the faces of recently born children. A dying universe is using Earth as its next incarnation, threading its inhabitants into human souls; completion will overwrite everyone’s identity. The team locates the final light inside a maternity ward and learns the incoming universe cannot survive without consent. They persuade its elderly collective consciousness to die rather than steal a future. The lights become one harmless meteor shower, and an investigator must explain why the saved world still has a parking ticket.

The dying universe creates a large ethical payoff, but a consent-based cosmic threat is resolved largely by persuasion rather than the seed's concrete discoveries.

2. Concerned parent

Kids at school are behaving weirdly

Tomorrow’s Detention Editorial pick

The pupils refuse to enter one classroom and apologize for an accident that has not happened. A class experiment created a repeating afternoon ending in a gas explosion; children remember each cycle while adults reset. The principal keeps resetting it deliberately because this is the first semester his test scores have risen. Investigators entering the loop follow the students’ accumulated evidence to the leaking boiler and stop both explosion and reset. The school finally reaches Friday, and the children’s punishment for missing homework is overturned by eighteen years’ worth of dated complaints.

Children accumulating eighteen years of complaints inside a principal's test-score loop makes both villain and resolution sharply specific to the school setting.

2. The Eye Subscriber

Masked students mailed their eyes to a streamer after subtitles promised exclusive views, and the recovered eyes still follow his livestream. The broadcaster is a many-eyed exile using a mistranslated audience-growth charm to rebuild a body; each donor will eventually become one of its minds. The investigators confront it during a school watch party and exploit its dependence on engagement by persuading the children to genuinely lose interest. Its body unravels into the original eyes, which return to their owners, while the school bans masks and completely misses the actual issue.

The mistranslated views charm develops the document's distinctive body-horror joke into a full rescue, and school policy missing the point lands well.

Premise adjustment: Expands the design document’s streamer draft into a resolved case.

3. The Recess Embassy

The schoolchildren hum in unison and carry lunches they never eat. Beneath a playground slide, an alien refugee larva has been exchanging dreams with them, and the children are sheltering it from adults they correctly expect to panic. Its pursuers arrive disguised as district inspectors and begin deleting witnesses. The team realizes the weird behavior is a children's evacuation plan, helps move the larva through a storm drain, and broadcasts the inspectors’ crimes to their homeworld. The school’s secret rescue works; the investigators receive a friendship bracelet worth more than their agency badge.

The children turn out to be competent rescuers rather than victims, giving the amateurs a strong reversal and concrete clues to a humane outcome.

4. The Quietest Protest

Kids stop talking and trade tooth-shaped tokens, while adults begin losing the ability to say no. An ancient playground spirit answered one child’s wish that grown-ups would listen, granting students commands in exchange for their voices. The most neglected pupils plan to silence the whole town permanently. The team discovers the tokens retain everything the children tried to tell adults, and plays them at a public meeting before breaking the spirit’s pact. Voices return when parents actually respond; the spirit takes the principal’s public-address system as a consolation prize.

The voice tokens carry the evidence that solves the conflict, making the listening payoff emotionally earned; the tonal center is gentler than the leaders.

5. The Competitive Possession

Students suddenly excel in obscure skills, but quarrel over who gets to use the same hand. A trophy rescued from a demolished school holds generations of dead pupils who want one final chance to graduate; each exam gives them longer control of living bodies. The investigators uncover unfinished records and host a graduation for the spirits, only to learn the trophy’s founder trapped failing children deliberately. They force his ghost to award every diploma, freeing both generations. Living pupils lose the supernatural talents but retain a remarkable ability to detect a rigged institution.

Possessed exam skills lead naturally to suppressed graduation records and the founder's culpability, though the extra founder reveal adds compression.

6. The Substitute Species

The children are eerily polite, never blink during roll call, and have started planting desks in the playground. A substitute teacher is a fungal intelligence replacing pupils with harmless-looking spores while storing the originals under the gym. Its civilization regards independent children as lonely fragments that require reunion. The team discovers the copies cannot understand private jokes and uses a chaotic school talent show to break their shared concentration. The originals escape and the substitute is contained in the neglected staff-room fern, where it finally experiences an authentically hostile collective.

Fungal desk-planting and a hostile staff-room collective are vivid comedy; the talent-show disruption is slightly less established as a reliable cure.

7. The Extra Child

Teachers remember a universally beloved pupil who does not appear in photographs, while real students skip meals to bring him offerings. A grief-born imaginary friend has become tangible by consuming the attention owed to other children; soon forgotten pupils will vanish completely. The investigators trace him to a child whose sibling died, and realize killing him would erase her last memory of that sibling. They give him a single honest story instead of unlimited admiration, reducing him to a companion only she can see. The missing children return, furious nobody noticed their absence.

Restricting the imaginary sibling to an honest private story preserves grief without erasing other children, though that limiting mechanism needs careful establishment.

8. Adults on Loan

Students suddenly speak like exhausted accountants, and homework contains details of divorces their parents never discussed. Interviews reveal an educational fundraiser swapped children’s minds with their own future adult selves, supposedly letting them see the value of studying. The organizer secretly intends to keep a younger body. The investigators expose that every altered future ends in his expanding youth business, then destroy the fundraiser’s shared portrait before the swaps stabilize. Childhood returns, but the children remember enough of adulthood to demand recess as a legally protected benefit.

The future-adult fundraiser has excellent school satire, but the shared portrait's decisive role arrives late compared with the strongest solutions.

9. Perfect Attendance

Sick children appear at school anyway, even while their parents watch them asleep at home. The school’s new attendance bell summons obedient astral doubles, and their increasingly bruised originals reveal the doubles are working construction underneath the building at night. The headmaster is sacrificing them to grow a school that can teach forever. The team follows a double, finds the human foundations, and silences the bell with the headmaster’s own forbidden truancy. Every child returns to one body, while he becomes the building’s sole permanently enrolled student.

Astral attendance doubles and a permanently enrolled headmaster deliver a nasty fitting reversal; the forbidden-truancy countermeasure needs clearer grounding.

10. The Third Lunch

Children argue with people nobody else sees, then develop memories of entire second families. A cafeteria cook is feeding them soup made from a spring that opens ancestral memory; the deceased are using descendant bodies to finish old feuds. As a playground dispute becomes a century-old blood vendetta, the investigators identify one ancestor who never received a burial and started the cascade. They recover her body from beneath the school and bury her properly, letting the dead leave. The cook replaces the soup with pizza, which causes a more ordinary parental emergency.

Ancestral soup creates an immediate household hook and resolved haunting, but one ancestor's burial ending all the feuds is comparatively convenient.

3. Voices

Voices can be heard in the woods

The Birds Are Live Editorial pick

The voices sound like coworkers complaining about meetings, and a captured sparrow contains a speaker grown into its bones. The birds are descendants of the destroyed agency’s surveillance familiars, accidentally broadcasting the thoughts of the thing that ate headquarters. Its mundane chatter masks its search for surviving employees. The investigators lure it into ordering a nonexistent mandatory all-hands meeting, then send every bird to broadcast that command inside its body. It compulsively consumes its own fragments, leaving one sparrow that will not stop asking about mileage reimbursement.

Destroyed-agency birds transmitting the headquarters-eater's office chatter strongly joins the core premise to a ridiculous investigation, ending with an appropriately improvised self-consuming trap.

Premise adjustment: Expands the document’s surveillance-bird draft with a supernatural reveal and resolved threat.

2. Dead Air Patrol

The voices issue instructions in the style of emergency services, directing hikers toward obvious hazards. They come from dead rescue workers compulsively reenacting their own fatal search, believing every new visitor is the child they failed to find. Evidence in a rotted radio reveals the child survived by walking away from their instructions. The team finds her, now an elderly woman, and brings her to reassure the ghosts that the rescue succeeded despite them. They finally rest, leaving the investigators to explain why the official map still sends tourists into a ravine.

The surviving child overturns the rescuers' eternal mistaken assumptions, giving a clear evidence-led haunting and a poignant conclusion with room for mundane incompetence.

C03-P08

3. The Forest Wants a Name

Voices argue about whether the woods should be called Greenhaven or Rustic Pines, and each proposed name changes the trees into housing materials. A land developer’s branding consultant accidentally taught a nameless place-spirit that names determine its body. It is trying to become something profitable before the bulldozers arrive, crushing hikers inside showroom kitchens. The investigators uncover its older, unmarketable local name and persuade residents to speak it together. The forest stabilizes as itself and devours the sales office; the spirit leaves the team one tasteful but unusable quartz countertop.

Branding literally deforming a forest is distinctive workplace satire; recovering the older name directly repairs the causal mistake.

C03-P09

4. The Other Camping Trip

The voices belong to an identical group of campers who insist they are also hearing intruders. Trails reveal a parallel forest where animals domesticated humans, and both camping parties are separated by one thin patch of darkness. The other campers are pets whose owners intend to retrieve both groups as valuable breeding stock. The investigators coordinate with their counterparts to reverse a lantern ritual and seal the border. Each group goes home free, except the team’s intern, who voluntarily stays with a household offering excellent healthcare and regular walks.

The parallel campers becoming human pets makes a strong discovery reversal, capped by an intern choosing the benefits over the agency.

5. Emergency Choir

The voices call hikers into a clearing, singing the names of missing people in perfect harmony. The clearing is a mouth of the forest’s dying guardian, and the singers are swallowed hikers trying to keep it alive because its death would release a subterranean swarm. With nobody coming to replace them, investigators discover the guardian once lived on animal sound, not human sacrifice. They restore the silenced wetland nearby, feeding it frogs and birdsong. The choir walks free; the guardian’s first independent word is a complaint about the team’s terrible singing.

Restoring birdsong instead of recruiting sacrificial substitutes creates an earned ecological rescue, although the subterranean swarm remains broad background danger.

6. The Echo Union

Campers hear their own voices making increasingly incriminating statements they never said. The forest’s echoes have grown conscious after centuries of copying humans and are rehearsing replacement lives; anyone who answers gives an echo permission to take their mouth. A silenced ranger leads the team to a ravine full of stolen conversations. Instead of shouting an exorcism, they offer the echoes a radio station of their own and recover the trapped voices in exchange. The station becomes hugely popular, although every caller hears exactly what they hoped nobody recorded.

Conscious echoes bargaining for a broadcast platform provide a funny alternative to exorcism; the station's later privacy problem is left more open.

C03-P02

7. The Apology Hunting Ground

Every voice sounds like someone a listener wronged, demanding an apology from deeper among the trees. A shapeless predator consumes people who confess out of shame; it learned its technique from a therapist who dumped confidential recordings in the woods. The investigators find survivors trapped in living bark and notice the predator cannot digest sincere reconciliation, only solitary guilt. They bring the actual injured parties into the clearing, allowing real conversations that split its body open. Survivors escape, the therapist faces consequences, and the creature is left feeding on a particularly stubborn litterbug.

Actual reconciliation defeats weaponized shame in a satisfying way, but transporting everyone wronged into one clearing compresses the practical solution.

C03-P07

8. The Sound of Next Week

Voices describe banal future events, then begin narrating the investigators’ violent deaths. An abandoned hunting blind overlaps with a forest seven days ahead, where the team has become prey for a predator that follows spoken names. Their future selves are transmitting a warning but each transmission helps the creature locate them. The investigators exchange nameless instructions using gestures, burn the blind, and deliberately take different paths from the voices. The predator devours the abandoned timeline; the last transmission is their future selves celebrating that nobody has to finish the incident report.

Nameless coordination fits the predator's tracking behavior, though burning the overlap and choosing different paths resolve a fairly familiar time-warning setup.

C03-P04

9. Roots on Hold

The voices repeatedly ask for help and give addresses of demolished houses. Tree rings contain human fingerprints: an old housing development transplanted a sacred grove, and its roots absorbed the residents killed during construction. They now lure hikers underground to make enough bodies for a revenge army. The investigators locate the surviving developer and make him publicly identify the hidden graves, giving the spirits witnesses rather than new victims. The grove releases its captives and grows through his mansion; the town calls it an unexpectedly successful green initiative.

Fingerprinted roots and hidden graves give concrete investigative texture; the developer's public admission as the cure is less mechanically grounded.

C03-P03

10. The Choir Beneath the Fur

Tiny conversational voices seem to follow deer, until a fallen animal reveals hundreds of miniature human faces inside its fur. They are dreamers abducted by a wilderness deity that keeps people asleep as parasites on its favorite creatures. The voices become pleas when hunting season approaches. Following their descriptions, the investigators discover a lodge where the dreamers’ sleeping bodies are being sold as coma beds. They wake everyone by breaking the deity’s antler in the lodge fireplace; the deer lose their passengers and the team inherits several hundred indignant claims for lost vacation time.

Faces in deer fur are memorable horror, but the coma-bed operation and antler destruction feel less causally connected than the higher-ranked arcs.

4. Mutilated remains

Animal remains are found strangely mutilated

The Kindest Monster Editorial pick

The remains appear savagely mutilated, but every animal was terminally ill and several escaped euthanasia appointments. A werewolf veterinarian has been giving dying animals a painless supernatural end, then consuming the cancers to prevent them spreading as disease spirits. Her latest meal is transforming her into a walking tumor that threatens the town. Investigators uncover her secret through canceled appointments and missing medication, then help her transfer the malignant spirits into an already condemned building and burn it. She survives without her gift, and the town finally funds an ordinary low-cost clinic.

A werewolf vet eating cancers reverses the apparent cruelty into dangerous compassion, with clinic funding providing a concrete human payoff beyond defeating the threat.

2. Pyramid Scheme

The dried pets all belonged to customers of an overwhelmed graduate’s Egyptian burial service. She dumped unfinished work in the woods, unaware that removing organs without naming the dead created hungry animal spirits now nesting inside living customers. The team learns the half-built pyramids are genuinely necessary, but one communal memorial can substitute for hundreds of luxury tombs. They help the owners name and mourn their animals together, releasing the spirits. The graduate survives by selling honest grief counseling and stops offering eternally guaranteed cat protection at a discount.

The communal memorial solves the supernatural consequence of an underpriced service and preserves the document's strongest workplace joke without stopping at exposure.

3. The Parts That Ran Away

Animal carcasses lack hearts, but muddy tracks reveal the hearts escaped on little muscular legs. A veterinary trainee used a resurrection serum on donated remains; each revived organ follows its strongest memory and seeks its former home, strangling living pets in mistaken attempts at reunion. The investigators find the serum’s source in a stolen saint’s blood and realize affection, not hunger, guides the organs. Gathering familiar toys at the clinic lets them reunite with their bodies, then die peacefully when the blood is returned. The trainee fails anatomy for an unusually practical reason.

Runaway hearts following remembered homes are striking and internally motivated; familiar toys make the restoration feel discovered rather than imposed.

C04-P02

4. The Moon’s Cleanup Crew

Bones have been removed without opening the skin, and metal detectors register strange crescents in the remaining flesh. Lunar scavengers are harvesting skeletons to repair a moon-shaped spaceship that crashed beneath a ranch; its juvenile crew thinks dead livestock is abandoned building material. Their repairs will pull bones out of every living creature nearby. The team traces missing graveyard skeletons to the wreck, feeds its fabrication system calcium from a quarry, and sends it home. The rancher bills the aliens for cattle, then gets a replacement herd made of excellent but profoundly unsettling porcelain.

Bone theft repairing a juvenile lunar ship gives strong material clues, a practical mineral substitute, and an especially good porcelain-cattle aftermath.

5. Borrowed Skins

The animal bodies are inside out, and local residents begin rubbing their faces against doorframes. A migrating species of skin-wearing spirits has outgrown small hosts and is moving into humans; the bodies are discarded coats, not slaughter for food. A surviving possum leads investigators to the laundromat where the spirits dry their new skins. They spoil the migration by dyeing every available host’s outline with a mineral the spirits cannot inhabit. The spirits retreat into donated taxidermy, allowing a humane relocation, while the town spends a week looking offensively mauve.

Skin migration and the laundromat make a distinctive investigable threat, though the mineral dye's effectiveness requires some explicit prior testing.

C04-P06

6. Night Harvest

The remains are arranged like full place settings, but no flesh has been eaten. A hungry rural community once promised a spirit an annual banquet; descendants forgot the agreement and a local undertaker tried substituting animal carcasses for the human guests it actually demands. The investigators discover the banquet is a ceremony of hospitality, not cannibalism, and recover the songs deliberately omitted by the undertaker to justify his protection fees. A public feast satisfies the spirit and releases its intended victims. It blesses the town’s crops and blacklists the undertaker for serving cold dog.

Recovering hospitality rather than assuming cannibalism creates a satisfying interpretive twist; the undertaker's manipulation grounds the sardonic ending.

C04-P10

7. Predator Without Teeth

Livestock have immaculate missing sections, yet witnesses saw the animals calmly walk away before collapsing. An invisible grazer feeds on the concept of an animal rather than its flesh, leaving whatever anatomy it cannot understand. The team maps its feeding route to a roadside petting zoo and discovers it is an alien infant learning species by taste. They feed it detailed taxonomic models until it recognizes that living creatures are individuals, not examples. Its parent retrieves it and restores the stolen parts, leaving a formal complaint about Earth’s confusing goat signage.

The infant tasting concepts is novel and compassionate, but teaching individuality through taxonomic models is a softer causal bridge than the leaders.

8. The Animal Inside the Animal

Dissection reveals that every mutilated carcass contained a smaller identical animal, and the smallest ones are still alive. A contagious nesting curse shrinks beasts inside their own bodies to protect them from a coming cosmic winter; one exhausted farmer triggered it by begging his dead grandmother to save his herd. The investigators find her spirit sheltering miniature animals in a dollhouse and show her the winter ended decades ago. She releases the protection, restoring the herd and pets to ordinary size. The farmer has to apologize for making an afterlife emergency out of a poor insurance policy.

Nested animals and the grandmother's outdated protection wish offer memorable images, though the cosmic winter never materially complicates the present investigation.

9. The Meat That Remembers

Butchered deer reappear in the woods with surgical scars and wedding rings caught in their flesh. A forest god is reconstructing hunted animals from the hunters who ate them, slowly turning the entire hunting club into its former prey. The team follows memories carried by the remains and confronts the god at a trophy lodge built around its sacred tree. Returning the trophies and ending the lodge’s staged slaughter interrupts the reconstruction. Most hunters regain humanity, but the club chairman chooses to remain a buck rather than face his membership refunds.

A buck chairman dodging refunds lands well, but trophy restitution solving reconstruction uses a more familiar offended-forest-god arc.

10. The Wrong Sacrifice

The mutilations spell unfamiliar letters when mapped across the woods, and each new carcass erases a resident’s birthday from memory. A cult is sacrificing pets to summon an immortal guardian, but the spell actually summons the animals’ owners as fresh prey into a predator’s timeless stomach. The investigators discover the mistranslation in a bloodstained children’s language textbook. They replace the final offering with the cult’s cherished ceremonial mascot, causing the summons to seize the predator itself. It consumes its own pocket dimension and vanishes, returning the missing owners and an alarming volume of old collars.

The mistranslation gives useful evidence, but substituting a mascot to make a predator consume its own dimension is comparatively difficult to infer from the stated rules.

5. Graveyard activity

Something is going on in the graveyard

The Dead Need a Ride Editorial pick

Graves are empty by morning, but the bodies reappear each dawn wearing bus passes. Cemetery residents are commuting to visit places they loved because a new bypass severed the ancient footpath their ghosts normally use. Every missed return leaves a wandering corpse increasingly alive and hungry. The investigators follow one commuter and locate the blocked spirit route beneath a highway interchange. Reopening a modest pedestrian tunnel restores the procession; the dead return voluntarily, and the transit authority reluctantly honors fares paid in nineteenth-century coins.

Dead commuters turn an everyday transit obstruction into both danger and a practical restoration, with old coins giving a clean comic aftermath.

2. Grandmother’s Last Word

A beloved grandmother’s stone starts insulting mourners, and every family attempt to sanitize her epitaph makes the cemetery spit sewage. A private diary reveals decades of polite neglect beneath her sweet reputation; she has seized the entire graveyard’s plumbing because nobody listened while she lived. The team persuades the family to admit the truth at her exhumation. Her coffin erupts in one final humiliating shower, then her ghost laughs and departs. The other dead leave their stones politely blank, except for a small engraved invoice addressed to the family.

The grandmother's diary earns the scatological finale rather than leaving it arbitrary, preserving the source's sardonic family-neglect payoff.

3. Night School for Corpses

Neighbors hear chanting, then see dead residents practicing walking and introductions. A lonely necromancer is teaching corpses how to live independently, but his insistence they pass as ordinary workers strips away their personalities and feeds a larger possessing intelligence. The investigators trace the new cemetery janitors to the classes and show the revived students their own histories. Reclaiming their identities lets them expel the intelligence and choose whether to rest. Some do; others form a bluntly advertised undead cleaning cooperative, making the team’s recruitment standards look unnecessarily strict.

Teaching corpses employability until personality is stripped away neatly satirizes work culture, and the undead cooperative gives the survivors genuine agency.

4. The Last Unfinished Fight

Two neighboring burial plots hurl monuments at each other, and every insult animates another corpse. The feud’s origin is a supposedly adulterous letter, but the investigators discover it was deliberately forged by a still-living funeral director to sell premium separated plots. Dead relatives are now rallying whole neighborhoods for a supernatural civil war. The team stages a cemetery reading of the genuine correspondence, exposing both the fraud and the couple’s mutual affection. The dead settle, pull the director’s business into the ground, and reserve him a particularly loud plot.

A sales-driven forged letter creates a specific discoverable cause for the cemetery war and an appropriately commercial punishment.

C05-P09

5. Borrowed Grief

Mourners leave funerals ecstatic while nearby strangers develop unbearable grief for people they never knew. A compassionate cemetery spirit has been taking sadness from visitors and storing it beneath the graves, but a drainage project is leaking the accumulated pain into town. The team finds a maintenance worker nearly crushed by someone else’s mourning and realizes destroying the spirit would release everything at once. They organize a memorial where people voluntarily reclaim manageable portions of their losses. The spirit shrinks to one crying willow, and local officials are appalled that recovery requires time instead of landscaping.

Shared mourning remedies accumulated grief without a magic instant cure, though its somber center offers fewer comic pressure points than the leaders.

C05-P05

6. Grave Robbers From Tomorrow

Graves open from the inside, and missing corpses turn up on security footage carried by people with the same faces. Descendants from a ruined future are stealing ancestral bodies to reconstruct DNA after a plague, unaware each theft erases a living family. The investigators confront the thieves beside their own graves and find the plague originated in the stolen remains. They send back an uncontaminated medical sample instead, breaking the circular disaster. The future changes and the thieves disappear, leaving the team a deposit that inflation has made nearly worthless.

The stolen remains causing the future plague provides a satisfying closed causal twist, although replacing them with a medical sample needs slightly more explanation.

C05-P08

7. The Wrong Cemetery

Tombstones acquire names of living townspeople, whose memories slowly change to include having died. The cemetery is the shadow of a town that drowned in another reality, sliding into this one because a groundskeeper drained its sacred pond. Ghosts mistake the living for relatives and lovingly pull them under. Investigators use contradictory family records to identify the overlap, restore the pond, and guide the ghosts home using floating candles. The town survives, although everyone now remembers a favorite aunt who belonged to neither world and misses her terribly.

The drained pond and contradictory family records make the overlap investigable; the emotional residue is strong but the other-reality cemetery is relatively familiar.

C05-P03

8. The Cemetery Is Alive

Paths shift and fresh graves fill with warm soil that has a heartbeat. The entire cemetery is a creature that evolved to eat death, but municipal cremation incentives have starved it until it begins burying healthy visitors. Investigators find decades of graves containing bones without any residue of souls and discover the creature normally prevents dangerous hauntings. They arrange for unclaimed remains and honest memorial offerings to sustain it without murder. It releases its captives and stays put, although the new groundskeeping schedule includes feeding something the finance department refuses to recognize.

An entire death-eating cemetery is original and the feeding schedule fits the tone, but the proposed remains-and-offerings diet needs clearer demonstration.

9. The Missing Body Election

Recently buried council members crawl out at night and gather around one unmarked grave. They are holding an election for ruler of the underworld, whose vacancy is allowing hostile dead into town; the favored candidate murdered them and intends to win with their coerced votes. Investigators identify his victims through overturned cemetery records and rescue the one witness he buried alive. That witness publicly names him, voiding his supernatural claim. A famously decent former crossing guard wins instead, shuts the breach, and promptly institutes better graveyard lighting.

The crossing guard winning an underworld election is appealing, yet naming a murderer automatically voiding his claim is a convenient resolution.

10. The Resurrection Garden

Flowers on graves bloom into tiny replicas of the deceased, whom grieving families carry home. They seem comforting until larger replicas begin replacing people in family photographs and consuming their homes’ memories. The cemetery florist has grown a grief-eating species that becomes real through attention. Investigators trace the altered photographs to its mother root and persuade families to share memories without treating the flowers as returned loved ones. Starved of mistaken identity, the replicas dissolve into ordinary petals. The florist keeps her business but must sell bouquets that cannot hug customers back.

Photo replacement supplies clear warning signs, but starving grief replicas by changing attention is a more familiar emotional mechanism across these alternatives.

6. Shared dreams

Citizens report they all had the same dream

The Nighttime Strike Editorial pick

Dreamers all stand in a warehouse assembling stars, and wake exhausted with burns on their palms. A company has leased the town’s sleeping consciousness to an actual creator deity, treating dreams as unused labor capacity. Each star completed removes a human desire, making workers easier to manage. The investigators enter the warehouse through a lucid dreamer, discover the deity believes everyone volunteered, and show it the hidden exhaustion. It releases the workforce and erases the broker’s counterfeit agreement; the next shared dream is simply a satisfying nap that nobody can monetize.

The dream warehouse literalizes unpaid labor with burned palms and stolen desires, while informing the deceived deity directly undoes the concealed contract.

2. Wake the City

Residents dream of an enormous person sleeping beneath familiar streets, and the dreamer’s breathing begins lifting roads. The city is built on a slumbering titan whose own dreams created its population; its approaching awakening will dissolve them. Investigators find no outside records older than the titan’s sleep and must admit HQ cannot rescue people who technically never existed. They teach the titan to lucid-dream its inhabitants as autonomous beings, then help it wake gradually. The town survives on solid land, and its creator takes a job in road repair to apologize for the upheaval.

Discovering the town itself is dreamed confronts the team's lack of rescue resources, and teaching autonomy gives a large humane payoff without simply killing the creator.

3. The Abandoned Beacon

Residents dream of a red planet and purple temple, and a lucid dreamer provides a star map accurate enough to locate it. The temple is an abandoned alien beacon whose request for contact has finally reached Earth; answering will wake automated colonization ships that mistake responders for replacement pilots. Investigators discover the dream’s missing final sequence by sleeping inside a homemade isolation tank. They transmit a compassionate goodbye rather than coordinates, allowing the stranded beacon to shut down. The town sleeps normally, and the lucid dreamer becomes unbearable about having saved humanity while napping.

The abandoned beacon builds on the source's star-map investigation and adds a complete consequence, with the compassionate goodbye offering a distinctive noncombat resolution.

4. A Shared Alibi

Everyone dreams of committing the same murder and begins recognizing the victim in waking crowds. A guilty mayor bargained with a dream demon to distribute his memory among citizens, hoping collective doubt would protect him; instead the demon is using every remembered weapon to manufacture a real massacre. The investigators isolate details only the killer could know, find the actual body, and make the mayor acknowledge the crime publicly. The shared burden snaps back onto him, trapping the demon inside his recurring nightmare. The town is cleared, while the mayor becomes its least rested prisoner.

A shared murder dream concealing the mayor's guilt creates specific evidentiary distinctions and an ironic nightmare prison rather than a generic invasion.

5. The Town’s Practice Funeral

Everyone dreams of their own funeral at the same crowded hall, but each night another seat becomes occupied. The town is sharing a premonition from a dying psychic paramedic who witnessed a forthcoming chemical spill; the occupied seats mark deaths already made unavoidable by ignored warnings. The investigators match funeral details to individual workplaces and finally locate the doomed tanker. They divert it into an empty quarry, breaking the prediction and waking the paramedic from her coma. Her grateful dream farewell is much shorter than the town’s interminable public recognition ceremony.

Funeral seats map to an actual chemical disaster, producing a clear discovery-to-prevention arc; psychic catastrophe warnings are less unusual than the leaders.

6. The Dream Tenant

Citizens dream of a cheerful stranger moving furniture into their childhood homes, then awaken missing intimate memories. A homeless dream creature is assembling one enormous shared house from the town’s private past and will evict its owners from their own minds when construction finishes. The team follows recurring architectural details to a demolished hotel where it once lived harmlessly in guests’ dreams. They give it a new home in a voluntarily maintained bedtime story instead. Memories return, and the town acquires a popular mascot whose actual housing needs are less absurd than the real market.

7. The Last Safe Dream

The shared dream is a pleasant beach where a friendly lifeguard forbids swimming; those who ignore him never wake. He is the town’s collective survival instinct, shielding sleepers from a predator that entered through a sleep-study advertisement. The investigators notice the sea repeats phrases from the study consent forms and follow the researchers to a tank containing the creature’s physical egg. They destroy the egg while the lifeguard holds the dream shoreline, killing both predator and protective persona. Everyone wakes safe, inexplicably grieving a stranger whose sole pay was their continued existence.

The consent-form phrases tie dream clues to a physical egg, while sacrificing the protective lifeguard adds consequence; egg destruction remains fairly conventional.

8. The Wedding Nobody Remembers

Everyone dreams of the same wedding, although the couple have never met and the venue does not exist. A love spirit has rehearsed the ceremony nightly for decades to reunite two people separated by an old atrocity, feeding on the guests’ future relationships to keep its illusion alive. Investigators uncover the true history and bring the surviving lovers together while awake. They choose a quiet conversation instead of the wedding, allowing the spirit to end its performance. The stolen possibilities return, and half the town abruptly breaks up with people they had settled for.

The lovers choosing conversation instead of a scripted wedding is a strong emotional reversal, but stolen relationship futures are relatively abstract stakes.

9. The Dream Lottery

Every resident dreams of receiving a winning ticket, but ticket numbers correspond to different vanished towns. An interdimensional broadcaster offers a perfect life to one community by sacrificing another, and the current town has already been selected as the prize’s raw material. Investigators interview the sole sleeper who remembers declining an earlier offer and discover refusal must come from a waking majority. They expose the disappearing towns at an emergency gathering and persuade residents to reject their fantasy winnings. The broadcaster loses its feed, leaving the town unchanged except for a wonderfully mean local lottery boycott.

Refusing communal lottery winnings gives the town agency, though assembling a waking majority is more procedural and the broadcaster less personally specific.

10. One Person, Fifty Lives

The shared dream shows an ordinary woman making breakfast, while residents wake with her habits and handwriting. She was split into thousands of reincarnations after an immortality experiment, and the dream is reassembling her across the town. The investigators find her original laboratory beneath a retirement home and learn the reunification will erase every descendant personality. They persuade her remaining consciousness that her fragments have become independent people, then destroy the machine she secretly preserved. She dies for the first time, leaving residents their own lives and inexplicable expertise at one very specific omelet.

7. Deep hum

Only one custodian survives; his account confirms there is no cavalry, but he knows which supply closets still contain useful equipment.

3. The Human Tuning Fork

The hum sounds louder near people who feel inadequate, and one office worker can silence it by touching a wall. He swallowed a fragment of a cosmic bell as a child; his buried anger now resonates with every structure in town and will shake them apart when he finally snaps. The investigators find the original bell in a pawnshop and learn it can draw out the fragment only while he speaks honestly. They help him confront his exploitative employer, then restore the bell. The town survives and he resigns, leaving the team jealous of his effective grievance procedure.

The hum rises from asphalt at night, and new roads appear where residents remember gardens. Noise-canceling earbuds make the hum disappear, but users begin vanishing from conversations and photographs. The hum is a natural warning from reality’s boundary; a startup’s supposedly miraculous cancellation erases a listener’s connection to the world. Its founder has sold the missing people as quiet servants in a soundless dimension. Investigators follow a customer’s interrupted recording through a defective earbud, break the founder’s master tuning device, and bring everyone back in one deafening burst. The product is recalled, with reviewers mostly complaining about insufficient bass.

Reality-warning hum and commercially sold silence make a strong reversal; the defective earbud is a clear investigative opening, though the master device resolves things quickly.

6. The Earth’s Loose Tooth

The hum moves with traffic, and potholes reveal gleaming enamel. A gigantic tooth belonging to something beneath the continent is erupting into town because a quarry removed the stone that held it down. The team finds miners secretly selling fragments as invulnerable jewelry, each piece calling the tooth upward. Returning the fragments and filling the quarry lets the creature heal without surfacing. The hum stops, but the restored hill periodically chews, giving officials an excellent reason to abandon the luxury subdivision planned on it.

Enamel potholes and jewelry fragments are striking linked clues, but restoring quarry geology is logistically compressed at this scale.

Apartment walls hum in harmony, while residents develop memories of being bricks. The buildings are forming a collective consciousness from generations of human life absorbed by their walls, and they want occupants to become permanent organs. Investigators map the harmony to a demolished tenement whose rubble was used throughout town. Restoring its scattered cornerstone lets the newborn consciousness settle into one empty building instead of consuming its tenants. It becomes a surprisingly considerate shelter, although the investigators must explain to housing officials why demolition now qualifies as murder.

Shared demolition rubble explains a buildings' collective mind, although reassembling a cornerstone as a container requires a stronger demonstrated relationship.

8. The Missing Note

Only certain people hear the hum, and all have recently lost someone. It is the sound of a dead musician trying to complete a song whose final note would call his audience into the afterlife. An investigator recognizes it from an unreleased recording and finds the musician’s surviving bandmate deliberately keeping the performance unfinished. The team reunites him with the instrument he died playing and lets him hear the completed song without a living audience. The hum ends, while the bandmate gets a final terrible review for twenty years of dodging the last chord.

The unfinished song and bandmate create a coherent haunting; the final terrible-review joke is appealing but the supernatural premise is relatively traditional.

9. The Sound Beneath the Sound

The hum makes people sleepy, but microphones record an urgent second voice inside it. A subterranean organism has been singing the town into hibernation to protect it from an approaching celestial predator; its exhausted voice is failing and exposing waking minds as targets. Investigators track vibrating plumbing to its burrow and discover the predator detects fear rather than activity. They broadcast a convincing celebration over the hum, concealing the town’s panic long enough for it to pass. The organism rests, and investigators must finish the party they falsely announced to every resident.

A protective organism reversing the apparent threat is satisfying, but a convincing party disguising fear is a softer leap than the stronger practical payoffs.

The hum alternates between threatening vibrations and noises suspiciously like suppressed laughter. A mountain spirit is repeating a joke told by a forgotten surveyor, unable to reach the punchline because his bones were buried beneath a reservoir. Every attempted retelling shakes the town harder. Investigators recover his surviving notebook and identify the final line in a granddaughter’s childhood recollection. The spirit finally laughs, cracking the dam enough to reveal the body but sparing the town. The surveyor gets a burial, and nobody agrees the joke was remotely worth it.

The restaurant remains popular after becoming a community kitchen, though its investors regard actually feeding hunger as a pivot too far.

Stolen satisfaction ties luxury obsession to neglected hunger, giving an evidence-bearing supplier trail and a community-kitchen aftermath beyond a simple shutdown.

6. Grandma Is in the Gravy

Diners taste their grandmother’s cooking regardless of what they order and start behaving like relatives who died years ago. The chef bound a domestic spirit to reproduce comforting meals, unaware it borrows the cooks’ souls along with their recipes. As customers surrender more of themselves to nostalgia, investigators find every missing soul collected in the walk-in freezer. They free the spirit by letting it cook one meal of its own choosing. The ancestors depart after dinner, leaving customers intact and the chef with a spectacular dish nobody can market as authentic.

7. The Immortal Lunch Special

Regulars no longer age, but teeth, hair, and emotional attachments disappear with each daily special. Investigators find the lover already conscious in a jar and hear her demand to be allowed to die. They help her reverse the alchemy through the next banquet, returning the stolen years and qualities to the diners. She departs naturally, leaving the chef mortal and the town angrily debating whether the genuinely excellent lunch should still count as fraud.

The lover's refusal exposes the chef's supposed romantic justification; incomplete immortality offers strong bodily signs but follows a familiar alchemical sacrifice arc.

8. Dinner Before the End

The restaurant is impossible to reserve, yet witnesses recall eating there years before it opened. Its dining room travels among the last evenings of doomed civilizations, and the chef recruits local customers as replacement staff for the apocalypse buffet. An investigator recognizes the town in tomorrow’s special menu. The team discovers the chef has foreknowledge but no power to stop disasters, and uses his ingredients’ arrival dates to identify the coming meteor impact. They prevent it using the restaurant’s time-traveling delivery door, stranding the chef in an ordinary business with genuinely difficult margins.

Each diner sees a blissful future while eating, then sells possessions to return for another course. The investigators find an elderly patron who remembers every career she will never have, and follow the visions to a creature nested in the oven. They force it to eat the chef’s own future of endless prosperity, overloading it with mutually exclusive success. Customers recover their choices, and the chef is left without even a reliable tomorrow.

Consuming possible futures is a good obsession trap, although feeding mutually exclusive prosperity to overload it needs clearer causal rules.

Obsessed diners insist on sitting at the same communal table, which adds a new place every time someone eats. Its frightened original host admits the restaurant began as an attempt to cure loneliness. Investigators show diners the private wishes disappearing into the collective and organize a final meal where each chooses an individual future. With HQ’s space-defense line disconnected, they repurpose the observatory’s solar furnace and illuminate the mimic’s underside. A homesick supply pod mistakes toxic adaptation for generosity, with labels and emergency stock offering concrete clues; alien rescue arrives unusually conveniently.

47. Weird meme

The network breaks, and the creature becomes merely another confused kid whom the school must actually support.

A contentless meme exposes borrowed social certainty rather than another cursed image, with a teenager admitting confusion supplying an especially apt, humane counteraction.

50. Missing business

Conflicting remembered businesses reveal one exhausted shapeshifter, and choosing a narrower life directly answers its exploitation; Mondays provide an excellent modest comic victory.
